Alka, you ask why your Bhupen Mama still gets up at six to go to the workshop. Listen. At twenty-five I made my first dovetail drawer that closed with a soft puff of air, no gaps, no glue showing. Old Mistry-ji tapped it and said, 'Hm. Not bad.' From him that was a medal. I carried that drawer home on the bus on my lap like a baby.
And you know what I felt the next morning? Hungry. I wanted to try a curved front, a hidden joint, a whole cabinet. I also looked at Mistry-ji's joints again and saw a hundred small things mine didn't have yet. It humbled me, but it didn't frighten me.
Two years of split wood had taught me one thing: the stuck months go somewhere. So I went back to the bench.

qa.a: He said, 'Hm. Not bad.'

qa.q: How did Bhupen feel the morning after making the drawer, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt proud and hungry for more, which shows in wanting to try a curved front, a hidden joint and a whole cabinet.

qa.a: It shows you can enjoy the pride, then look honestly at what still remains to learn and go back to steady practice without fear.

The rain started as Pema turned off the main road at Ghoom, a thick grey sheet that swallowed the tea gardens. Varun, in the passenger seat, gripped the door handle out of habit.
Six months ago she had stalled on this exact slope four times while a jeep honked behind her. Today her feet did it without asking: clutch, a touch of gas, handbrake off. The car rolled up the hill and she let out a laugh.
'You're actually good at this now,' Varun said.
'I know,' she said, and grinned. Then, more quietly, 'Next I want to try the night drive down to Siliguri. And I still can't reverse into a tight spot. There's so much left.'
She said it without the old dread. The stalling months had got her here; the next ones would get her somewhere too. The wipers thumped steadily.

qa.a: She had stalled on this exact slope four times.

qa.a: She could practise reversing and driving with an experienced driver like Varun beside her before trying the night drive to Siliguri.

qa.a: Varun still grips the handle out of habit, but he is impressed and can tell she is truly skilled now.

"And then it clicked, months later. So fingerstyle? I'll be terrible for a while. Fine. I know terrible leads somewhere now."
"Can I keep the price tag as a souvenir?"
"Frame it," Kamal said, grinning.

Last Friday I gave the site safety briefing in Hindi. Twelve minutes, forty workers, and nobody laughed at the wrong moment. When I moved from Kochi to Delhi two years ago I couldn't order tea without pointing. Keerthana from the planning team used to translate for me in meetings, and I hated how small that made me feel.
After the briefing an old mason came up and asked something fast, full of words I'd never heard. I understood maybe half. So there's that.
I felt proud walking to the canteen. I also felt, strangely, hungry. I want to understand the jokes the crew makes at lunch, not just the safety terms. That's a whole new mountain.
Two years ago that thought would have crushed me. Now I've just bought a second notebook. I know how the first one ended.
Joseph

qa.a: Twelve minutes, to forty workers.

Instructor's note, Saturday session
Bidisha topped the grey overhang route today, the one that has thrown her off at the third hold since March. Karthik was belaying. When she lowered down she was shaking and grinning and said "Did you see that?" about four times.
Twenty minutes later I found her staring at the orange route beside it, the hardest on our wall, tracing holds in the air with a finger. She asked me its grade and then said, "Okay. That'll take me a year. Maybe two." No drama in it, just a plan.
What stood out: in March she used to leave early after a fall. Today she asked Karthik to film her attempts on the orange so she could study her falls.
Next step from me: I've added her to the Tuesday advanced group for footwork drills.

qa.q: Which route did Bidisha top today?
qa.a: The grey overhang route.

qa.q: What does Bidisha tracing holds on the orange route suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: She feels proud and eager for a harder challenge, yet calm and humble about needing a year or two.

qa.q: What did the instructor do next, and why does it suit this stage?
qa.a: The instructor added Bidisha to the Tuesday advanced group for footwork drills, giving her new hunger structured practice.

qa.q: What might Karthik have noticed while belaying and filming?
qa.a: Karthik likely saw Bidisha's joy at the top and her new calm about falling, since she now wants her falls filmed to study them.

grounding: An instructor's note shows a climber's pride after a hard route turning into hunger for the next level and calm trust in the struggle.

Sunday.
Sold out! All twenty-four croissants gone from the market table by 10:30. Eight months ago my first batch came out like buttery bricks. I have photos to prove it.
I'm so proud I keep smiling at nothing. Vishal teased me all the way home: "Bhavna, now you'll want to open a café." Maybe, one day. What I actually want next is brioche, and a proper sourdough, and to understand why my layers still smear on hot days.
Funny thing: the better I get, the more I see how much I don't know. The baker at the next stall glanced at my croissants and said, kindly, "Nice. Your dough's a bit warm." A year ago that would have crushed me. Today I just asked, "How do you keep it cold?" I know now that the stuck months lead somewhere. I've lived it.

qa.a: All twenty-four croissants were gone by 10:30.

qa.a: Bhavna felt curious rather than crushed, and asked how to keep the dough cold.
